items.item: The end-to-end argument says a function correct only with the application's own knowledge can be completely and correctly implemented only at the endpoints; a lower layer's attempt at the same function can be a useful performance optimisation but never a substitute.

On a fair-loss link, the only way to be reasonably sure a message arrives is to retry it, and a retry sent after a lost acknowledgement delivers the message twice; at-most-once is the choice never to retry, risking loss instead of duplication, and there is no third option.

at.step: Reveal: at-least-once is the best a lossy link offers

items.item: Running the identical retry with no idempotency key lets a processor apply both the original request and the retry as two separate charges; sending the same idempotency key on both attempts lets the processor recognize the second as a repeat of the first and apply it as a no-op.

at.step: Reveal: the shop's charge, twice without a key, once with one

items.item: Exactly-once names an effect, not a stronger delivery mechanism: delivery remains at-least-once throughout, and what changes is that an idempotent write makes applying the message twice cost the same as applying it once.

at.step: Reveal: exactly-once as an effect, not a delivery guarantee

items.item: Kafka transactions commit a producer's output records and the consumer's offsets together as one atomic unit, and Flink's TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction pre-commits an external write at a checkpoint and only commits it once that checkpoint succeeds; both close the same crash window by making two writes one unit.

at.step: Reveal: making consume, produce and record-the-offset one atomic unit

items.item: A table-format commit's atomic pointer swap is a third version of the identical atomic-commit idea, already taught in this chapter; none of the three atomic-commit mechanisms reach an effect that has already left the system, such as a sent email or an external charge made outside the pipeline's own transaction.

at.step: Reveal: where the pipeline stops being able to help

items.item: An idempotency key makes a retry safe only for the specific write that checks it; a second, unrelated side effect triggered by the same retried request, such as a confirmation email with no deduplication of its own, still happens again even after the key is added.

at.step: Prove it: an idempotency key is added everywhere — is retrying now always safe?

items.item: A deterministic computation whose inputs can be replayed can recover from a failure by overwriting its prior, partial output with the freshly recomputed one, rather than appending the new result alongside the old as a second copy.

at.deep: Lab: an atomic commit is "no observable in-between," not "no failure"
